About this citation

Citations of the Apology in this archive are locators in Plato's dialogue, in which Socrates speaks. The archive files the passage under Socrates because he is the thinker being quoted, but Plato wrote the work, and the citation therefore names Plato and the page says who is speaking. The English wording is the translator's, so the locator identifies the passage while the quoted sentence belongs to a particular rendering of it.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“What I do not know, I do not claim to know.”

Ancient Greek

“ἃ μὴ οἶδα οὐδὲ οἴομαι εἰδέναι.”

Literally “what I do not know, I do not think I know either.” The archive's English rendering compresses this to a claim about claimed knowledge.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “I know that I know nothing.”
-   “I know one thing: that I know nothing.”

### Attribution notes

“I know that I know nothing” is a later compression, not a sentence in Plato. The Apology passage is narrower and more careful: Socrates claims only that where he lacks knowledge he also does not believe he has it. The popular version turns a claim about his own position into a paradox about knowledge in general.

#### About Socrates

Socrates (c. 470/469–399 BCE) was an Athenian citizen who wrote nothing and yet redirected Greek philosophy from cosmology toward ethics and the care of the soul.

### Interpretation

The sentence summarises Socrates' position at his trial rather than quoting Plato directly: after consulting politicians, poets, and craftsmen, he concludes that his superiority consists solely in not claiming knowledge he lacks. The claim is methodological, not sceptical. Socrates does not deny that knowledge is possible; he denies that he has it, and treats that denial as the starting point of inquiry. The Oracle's saying that no one is wiser becomes, on his reading, a reason to keep examining.

#### Why it matters

The distinction worth keeping is between holding a view and knowing it. Most disagreements would shrink if people stated which of the two they were doing.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “What I do not know, I do not…”?

“What I do not know, I do not…” comes from Apology, 21d (later paraphrase of the idea) (c. 399–390 BCE), attributed to Socrates.

#### What does Socrates mean by knowledge?

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge, humility, wisdom.

#### Is the wording of this Socrates quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “What I do not know, I do not claim to know.” Forms in circulation that differ: I know that I know nothing. / I know one thing: that I know nothing. The Ancient Greek reads “ἃ μὴ οἶδα οὐδὲ οἴομαι εἰδέναι.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

“I know that I know nothing” is a later compression, not a sentence in Plato. The Apology passage is narrower and more careful: Socrates claims only that where he lacks knowledge he also does not believe he has it. The popular version turns a claim about his own position into a paradox about knowledge in general.
